title: Kashmir Shaivism opening (the Shiva Sutras)
hook: a run of short lines in the Shiva Sutras turns the self into a dancer, the inner self into a stage, and the senses into the audience

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kashmir Shaivism opening, a thread of the Shiva Sutras said wonder marks the stages of yoga. Which ordinary thing surprised you? A new week starts in the same book. Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.
screen: `THE SHIVA SUTRAS.` · `A NEW WEEK, THE SAME BOOK.`

segments.voice: On a lit stage, one dancer becomes a lover, then a king, then a frightened deer, then a god. The face changes, the hands change, and it's the same dancer the whole time. The Shiva Sutras turn that picture inward in three very short lines. Nartaka atma: the self is a dancer. The stage is the inner self. The spectators are the senses. No story, no argument. Just a theater, built in three breaths. Some days back, Nataraja danced in bronze, in a ring of fire. Here the dance moves indoors.
screen: `ONE DANCER, MANY ROLES.` → `NARTAKA ATMA.` → `A THEATER, INDOORS.`

segments.voice: Start with the dancer. In Kashmir Shaivism, there is one consciousness, and it's Shiva's. On this view, everything a person is, is that consciousness playing a part. Like the dancer on that lit stage, the self takes on roles: a worker, a parent, a worried person at a red light. It plays each one fully. Then the stage. The line says the stage is the inner self, the antaratma. The play doesn't happen out there somewhere. It happens inside, on the floor of your own awareness, where thoughts and moods step out and take a bow. Then the audience. The senses are the spectators. Your eyes, your ears, your skin: they sit in the seats and watch the show. Put the three lines together and something shifts. Commentators in the tradition read this as a description of someone who has woken up. Not someone who quits the roles. Someone who plays them, all of them, and never forgets who's dancing. The anger at a coworker still comes on stage. The tenderness toward a child still comes on stage. But the one in the costume knows it's a costume. A dancer who forgets they're performing gets lost in the part. A dancer who remembers can play a tragedy all evening and walk home whole. That's the invitation in these lines. Not to stop the dance. To dance it awake.
screen: `THE SELF IS A DANCER.` · `THE STAGE IS THE INNER SELF.` · `THE SENSES ARE THE AUDIENCE.` · `PLAYING A PART, AWAKE.` · then, large: `NEVER FORGET WHO'S DANCING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the stage. Sit, and let the eyes close or rest on the floor. Let the breath do what it does. Now name a few roles you've already played today. The one who got up. The one who answered a message. The one who was short with someone, or kind. Let each one step onto the inner stage, take its bow, and step off. You don't have to judge them. Just notice the one who's watching, who was there for every role. If you pray, you can offer the whole performance to Shiva. The bell holds the time.
Kashmir Shaivism opening, the Shiva Sutras. Today's lines: the self is a dancer, the stage is the inner self, the spectators are the senses.
Your line: Kashmir Shaivism opening, the Shiva Sutras. Today, when you step into a role, at work, at home, on the phone, notice the moment you walk onstage. Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Students of Kashmir Shaivism study the Shiva Sutras line by line, usually with a traditional commentary, and some memorize and recite the sutras in Sanskrit.

fork.setup: you're in the middle of a hard role today: the patient parent, the calm coworker. in the sutras' picture, what does the awake dancer do?
options: drop the role, since it's only a costume.
play it fully, remembering who's dancing.
fork.reveal: the tradition reads the dancer as someone who plays every part fully and never forgets the one wearing the costume.

original.note: Sanskrit: dancer. the line nartaka atma means the self is a dancer.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty metaphor about life being a play.
what it means: one consciousness plays every role; the inner self is the stage, the senses are the audience.
